symbols.jewish: Repeats 13:10 and 12:17. Keeping God's commandments recalls the covenant at Sinai; the faith of (or in) Jesus stresses loyalty to Christ. Daniel 12:12 blesses those who endure.
symbols.meaning: The warnings of 14:9-11 serve pastoral exhortation: believers must endure rather than compromise. Whether 'faith of Jesus' means faith in Jesus or faithfulness like his is debated grammatically.

symbols.phrase: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from this moment on; they will rest from their labors, for their deeds will follow them
symbols.jewish: The second of seven beatitudes in Revelation. Rest for the righteous dead appears in Isaiah 57:1-2 and Daniel 12:13; Hebrews 4 develops the Sabbath rest of God's people. 4 Ezra 7:35 and 2 Baruch 14:12 speak of works or righteous deeds accompanying the righteous. A later rabbinic saying (Pirqe Avot 6:9) says that at death neither silver nor gold accompanies a person, only Torah and good deeds.
symbols.cultural: Greco-Roman epitaphs often expressed resignation or hopelessness about death ('I was not, I was, I am not, I do not care'); John promises blessing and rest.
symbols.meaning: Martyrs and all who die faithful are blessed: their toil ends and their faithful works are remembered by God. 'From now on' (ap' arti) marks the present era of persecution.

readings.reading: A special comfort to believers dying in the coming Neronic and Jewish War crises, and to all believers thereafter (Gentry).
Especially the martyrs of the tribulation (Walvoord).
All believers who die faithful in any age (Hendriksen).

symbols.phrase: One like the Son of Man seated on a white cloud, with a golden crown on His head and a sharp sickle in His hand
symbols.jewish: Daniel 7:13-14: one like a son of man comes with the clouds to receive everlasting dominion. Jesus applied this to himself (Mark 14:62; Matthew 24:30). Clouds are the vehicle of divine presence and judgment (Exodus 13:21; Psalm 104:3; Isaiah 19:1). Joel 3:13 commands, 'Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe.'
symbols.cultural: The golden crown (stephanos) was the victor's wreath and the triumphing general's crown; Roman emperors wore golden wreaths in triumphs.
symbols.meaning: Most identify the figure as Christ, the victorious Son of Man (compare 1:13). A minority argue that he is an angel because he receives instruction from 'another angel' (14:15); responders note that the angel merely relays God's timing, as Christ himself said only the Father knows the hour (Mark 13:32).

readings.reading: Christ coming in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70 (Matthew 24:30; 26:64) and gathering his elect (Chilton, Gentry).
Christ's final judgment at the end of the historical sequence the book has traced (Barnes).
Christ's second coming at the end of the tribulation (Walvoord, Thomas).
Christ's final coming in judgment at the end of history (Hendriksen, Beale).

symbols.phrase: Swing Your sickle and reap, for the crop of the earth is ripe; the earth was harvested
symbols.jewish: Joel 3:13 pairs grain harvest and winepress as judgment on the nations in the valley of decision. Jesus uses harvest for the gathering of the righteous at the end of the age (Matthew 13:30, 39-43; Mark 4:29; John 4:35-38). Grain harvest in Israel (barley, wheat) came in spring and early summer, celebrated at Passover/Firstfruits and Pentecost.
symbols.cultural: Harvest was the economic heart of agrarian Asia Minor; reaping with sickles was a universal image of death (later the Grim Reaper).
symbols.meaning: Commentators divide on whether the grain harvest (14:14-16) is the ingathering of the righteous, followed by the vintage of judgment (14:17-20), or whether both are judgment as in Joel 3:13. Since the term 'firstfruits' was just used of believers, many see a positive harvest of the saints; others note the 'dried up' or 'ripe' (xeraino) language suggests judgment.

readings.reading: The gathering of the elect through the gospel and the judgment on Israel at the end of the old-covenant age (Chilton).
Separating the righteous and wicked at Christ's return; many dispensationalists read both harvests as judgments at Armageddon (Walvoord).
The final gathering of God's people at the last judgment, paired with the judgment of the wicked (Beale, Bauckham).

symbols.phrase: Another angel came out of the temple; still another, with authority over the fire, came from the altar
symbols.jewish: The altar in Revelation is where the souls of martyrs cry out for justice (6:9-11) and where the incense of the saints' prayers rises before fire is thrown on the earth (8:3-5). The perpetual fire of the altar (Leviticus 6:12-13) and coals from the altar used in judgment (Ezekiel 10:2) lie behind 'authority over the fire'.
symbols.meaning: The vintage of judgment comes from the heavenly temple and altar, so it is God's answer to the martyrs' prayers. Jewish tradition assigned angels to elements (1 Enoch 60:11-21; Jubilees 2:2), and Revelation has angels of the winds (7:1) and waters (16:5).

symbols.phrase: Gather the clusters of grapes from the vine of the earth, because its grapes are ripe
symbols.jewish: Israel is God's vine or vineyard (Isaiah 5:1-7; Psalm 80:8-16; Jeremiah 2:21; Hosea 10:1), and Jesus is the true vine (John 15). The 'vine of Sodom' (Deuteronomy 32:32-33) produces poisonous grapes. Joel 3:13 calls for treading the full winepress of the nations.
symbols.cultural: Grape harvest (vintage) came in late summer and autumn and was celebrated with festivals of Dionysus in the Greek world; Asia Minor's valleys were famous wine country. In Judaism the autumn vintage coincided with the festival of Tabernacles (ingathering).
symbols.meaning: The 'vine of the earth' (or 'of the land') stands in contrast to the true vine: it is humanity organised in rebellion and ripe for judgment.

readings.reading: The 'vine of the land': apostate Israel, the vineyard that produced bad fruit (Isaiah 5), judged in AD 70 (Chilton).
The ungodly nations gathered against Christ at Armageddon (Walvoord).
Unbelieving humanity in rebellion, ripe for final judgment (Beale, Hendriksen).

symbols.phrase: The great winepress of God's wrath was trodden outside the city
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 63:1-6 pictures the LORD returning from Edom with garments stained red from treading the winepress of the nations alone; Lamentations 1:15 says the Lord trod Judah like grapes in a winepress; Joel 3:2, 12-14 places the nations' judgment in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, traditionally the Kidron valley outside Jerusalem; Zechariah 14:2-4 has the nations gathered against Jerusalem. Executions took place outside the camp or city (Leviticus 24:14; Numbers 15:35), as did Jesus' crucifixion (Hebrews 13:12).
symbols.cultural: Ancient winepresses were stone vats where grapes were trodden by foot, the juice flowing down a channel; red juice splashing on clothes made the image of blood vivid. Roman sieges ended with mass slaughter outside the walls: Josephus describes the crucifixion of thousands of captives outside Jerusalem during the siege (Jewish War 5.446-451).
symbols.meaning: God's judgment of rebellious humanity is complete and terrible. Revelation 19:15 shows Christ treading this winepress. 'The city' is probably Jerusalem or the holy city (the beloved city of 20:9), i.e. God's people are protected inside while judgment falls outside; others see it as Babylon.

readings.reading: The destruction of the Jewish nation in AD 70, with slaughter around Jerusalem and throughout the land (Chilton, Gentry).
The battle of Armageddon, centred on the land of Israel around Jerusalem (Walvoord, Thomas).
The final judgment on the ungodly, while the 'city' of God's people is safe (Beale).
Final judgments on the enemies of the church at the end of the historical sequence (Barnes).

symbols.phrase: The blood rose as high as the bridles of the horses
symbols.jewish: Jewish apocalyptic used this hyperbole for eschatological slaughter: 1 Enoch 100:3 says a horse will walk up to its chest in the blood of sinners, and 4 Ezra 15:35-36 speaks of blood up to a horse's belly. Later rabbinic tradition (y. Taanit 4:8; Lamentations Rabbah 2:2) described blood reaching the horses' nostrils at Bethar in the Bar Kokhba revolt (135), a later but parallel idiom.
symbols.cultural: Josephus reports that during the sack of Jerusalem the alleys ran with blood that quenched fires (Jewish War 6.406), which preterists cite as a fulfilment.
symbols.meaning: Deliberately hyperbolic battle imagery for the totality of judgment, not a literal measurement; some futurists take it more literally.

readings.reading: The slaughter of the Jewish War, as described by Josephus (Chilton).
The great bloodshed of Armageddon; some futurists take it literally in places, others as hyperbole or spattering blood (Walvoord, Thomas).
A conventional apocalyptic image for complete judgment (Beale, Bauckham).

symbols.phrase: For a distance of 1,600 stadia
symbols.jewish: 1,600 is 40 x 40 or 4 x 4 x 100. Four is the number of the earth (four corners, four winds, Revelation 7:1), and forty recalls periods of judgment and testing (the flood, the wilderness). Jerome noted that the length of Palestine from Tyre to the Egyptian border was about 160 Roman miles, close to 1,600 stadia.
symbols.cultural: A Greek stadion was about 185-192 metres, so 1,600 stadia is about 300 kilometres (some 184-190 miles). Distances measured in stadia were standard in Greek geography and in Josephus.
symbols.meaning: The number signals judgment that covers the whole earth (4 squared, multiplied). A match with the approximate length of the land of Israel is noted by many, and fits preterist and futurist readings that tie the judgment to the land.

readings.reading: The length of Palestine: the judgment covers the whole land of Israel in the Jewish War (Chilton).
A literal region, roughly the length of Israel, over which the Armageddon campaign extends (Walvoord, Thomas).
A symbolic number for universal, complete judgment over the four corners of the earth (Beale, Hendriksen).
Usually symbolic of extensive judgment on the papal or antichristian realm (Barnes).

The 144,000 are the first-century Jewish-Christian firstfruits; the three angels announce the gospel to the world before the judgment on Jerusalem; Babylon is apostate Jerusalem (or Rome for some); the harvest and winepress depict the gathering of the elect and the destruction of the Jewish nation in AD 70, whose bloodshed covered the land (1,600 stadia, the length of Palestine) (Chilton, Gentry).

Reads the harvest of 14:14-20 as the final coming of Christ in AD 70, in which the end of the age, the judgment and the resurrection were fulfilled; critics regard this as incompatible with the creedal hope of a future bodily return, while proponents argue the New Testament's time-texts demand it.

The 144,000 are the faithful church during papal supremacy; the three angels are successive movements in history: the Reformation and missionary proclamation, the Protestant identification of papal Rome as fallen Babylon, and a final warning; Seventh-day Adventists identify them with the advent message beginning in the 1840s; the harvests are the climax of history (Elliott, Barnes, Uriah Smith).

A preview of the tribulation's climax: the 144,000 Jewish believers stand with Christ on the literal Mount Zion at his return; literal angels proclaim the gospel and warn against the mark; the harvest and winepress depict the battle of Armageddon in the land of Israel (Walvoord, Thomas).

A pastoral counterpoint to chapter 13: the church, secure with the Lamb, must persevere because Babylon's fall and the final judgment are certain; the two harvests depict the end of history, the gathering of the saints and the judgment of the wicked (Hendriksen, Milligan).

Beale, Bauckham and Osborne read the 144,000 as the whole church depicted as a holy army, the three angels as a final call and warning, and the harvests as the last judgment, with first-century Rome as the immediate face of Babylon and the end of history as the horizon.

questions: How does the picture of the 144,000 on Mount Zion function as a reply to the beast and its marked followers in chapter 13?
Is the grain harvest of 14:14-16 a gathering of the righteous or a judgment of the wicked? What clues in the text and in Joel 3 point each way?
Why might John announce Babylon's fall here before describing her in chapters 17-18, and how do the identifications (Rome, Jerusalem, papal Rome, a future system) change the warning?
How should the severe warning of 14:9-11 be read alongside the beatitude of 14:13 and the call to perseverance in 14:12?
What do the Old Testament harvest and winepress texts (Joel 3, Isaiah 63) contribute to understanding the scale and nature of judgment here?
